blurb: How chips are made: ultra-pure silicon, EUV lithography, new transistor shapes, and why it's all geopolitics.

cards.title: Making the canvas

steps.p: Quartz sand is reduced to silicon and then refined until roughly one atom in a billion is a contaminant.
A seed crystal is dipped into molten silicon and slowly pulled up while rotating (the Czochralski process), growing a single-crystal ingot.
The ingot is sawn into wafers less than a millimeter thick and polished to near-atomic flatness. Hundreds of chips are then built on each wafer.

cards.aside: A perfect, uninterrupted crystal lattice matters because defects scatter electrons and kill transistors.

cards.q: What diameter wafer do leading-edge fabs use today?
cards.why: 300 mm. It has been the standard since the early 2000s. A move to 450 mm was planned around 2012 but abandoned because re-tooling the whole industry cost too much.

cards.statement: A transistor is essentially a switch that electricity can turn on and off.
cards.why: True. In a MOSFET, voltage on the gate creates or removes a conducting channel between source and drain. Billions of these switches, combined, implement all digital logic.

cards.q: Adding phosphorus atoms to silicon (doping) makes it…
cards.why: n-type. Phosphorus has five outer electrons to silicon's four, so one is left free to move. Boron, with three, creates holes and makes p-type silicon. Junctions between the two are the basis of transistors.

cards.title: Electronic-grade silicon is around 99.9999999% pure — "nine nines".
cards.detail: That is roughly one foreign atom per billion silicon atoms, far purer than solar-grade silicon. Even trace metals at this level can ruin transistor behavior.

cards.statement: Moore's law is a law of physics.
cards.why: False. It is an observation and an industry target. Gordon Moore noted in 1965 that transistor counts doubled yearly, revised it to every two years in 1975, and the industry organized its roadmaps to keep it true.

cards.title: How patterns get onto silicon

steps.p: The wafer is coated in light-sensitive photoresist. Light shines through a patterned mask, shrunk by optics, onto the resist.
Exposed (or unexposed) resist is washed away, and the uncovered material is etched or implanted. The resist is then stripped.
A modern chip needs dozens of such patterned layers, each aligned to the previous one within a few nanometers.

cards.aside: The smallest feature you can print scales with the wavelength of light, which is why the industry chased shorter wavelengths for decades.

cards.q: Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography uses light with a wavelength of about…
cards.why: 13.5 nm. The previous workhorse, deep ultraviolet, uses 193 nm. The 14× shorter wavelength lets fabs print fine features in a single exposure instead of multiple patterning passes.

cards.q: Which company is the only supplier of EUV lithography machines?
cards.why: ASML, based in the Netherlands. Each machine costs well over $150 million, and it relies on suppliers such as Zeiss for mirrors and Trumpf for its lasers.

cards.statement: EUV light passes through glass lenses just like visible light.
cards.why: False. EUV is absorbed by almost everything, including air and glass. Machines run in vacuum and focus with multilayer mirrors, each reflecting only part of the light.

cards.title: EUV light is made by hitting molten tin droplets with a laser around 50,000 times per second.
cards.detail: Each droplet is struck twice — once to flatten it, once to vaporize it into a plasma that emits 13.5 nm light. Very little of the input energy ends up as usable light.

cards.statement: The "3 nm" in a 3 nm process refers to the size of a transistor's gate.
cards.why: False. Node names became marketing labels long ago. No physical feature on a "3 nm" chip is 3 nm; gate pitches are several times larger. Compare densities, not names.

cards.title: From flat to fins to nanosheets

steps.p: As flat transistors shrank, the gate lost control of the channel underneath, and current leaked even when switched off.
Raising the channel into a vertical fin let the gate wrap three sides, restoring control. Intel shipped them first, around 2011–2012.
Stacked horizontal nanosheets let the gate surround the channel completely. Samsung, TSMC and Intel are moving to these at their newest nodes.

cards.aside: Each shape change was about one thing: keeping the switch from leaking as it shrank.

cards.q: What mainly forced the move away from planar transistors?
options: Leakage — the gate could no longer fully turn the channel off
They were too slow to manufacture
cards.why: Leakage. At short channel lengths, the drain's field competes with the gate. Off-state current and power climb, so a better-wrapped gate was needed.

cards.q: The end of Dennard scaling in the mid-2000s meant that…
options: Shrinking transistors no longer kept power density constant, so clock speeds stalled
cards.why: Power density stopped falling. Voltages could not keep dropping, so faster clocks meant more heat. That is why CPUs plateaued near 3–5 GHz and the industry went multicore.

cards.statement: Intel was the first company to ship FinFET transistors in volume.
cards.why: True. Intel's 22 nm "Tri-Gate" process in Ivy Bridge CPUs (2012) was the first high-volume FinFET product. TSMC and Samsung followed a few years later.

cards.title: NVIDIA's H100 GPU packs about 80 billion transistors onto one die.
cards.detail: Its Blackwell successor exceeds 200 billion by joining two dies at the reticle limit — the largest area a lithography scanner can expose in one shot.

cards.q: "Backside power delivery" moves which wiring underneath the transistors?
cards.why: Power. Normally power and signal wires compete for space above the transistors. Feeding power from below frees the top for signals and reduces voltage drop. Intel calls its version PowerVia.

cards.title: Who makes what

steps.p: Companies like NVIDIA, Apple, AMD and Qualcomm design chips but own no factories. They are called fabless.
TSMC, founded by Morris Chang in Taiwan in 1987, pioneered manufacturing chips for others. Samsung and Intel also offer foundry services.
A few firms dominate key steps: ASML in lithography, Applied Materials, Lam and Tokyo Electron in deposition and etch, Japanese firms in photoresists.

cards.aside: No single country controls the whole supply chain, which is exactly what makes it a strategic issue.

cards.q: Which of these companies is fabless?
cards.why: NVIDIA. It designs GPUs and has them manufactured mostly by TSMC. Intel and Samsung run their own fabs; TSMC is the foundry itself.

cards.statement: Most of the world's most advanced logic chips are manufactured in Taiwan.
cards.why: True. TSMC's Taiwan fabs produce the large majority of leading-edge chips, including most AI accelerators. New fabs in Arizona, Japan and Germany are meant to diversify that.

cards.q: TSMC's CoWoS packaging became a bottleneck for AI chips. What does it do?
options: Places GPU dies and HBM stacks side by side on a silicon interposer
cards.why: Advanced packaging. CoWoS (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate) connects the GPU to its HBM through thousands of tiny wires in a silicon layer. Capacity for it, not just wafers, has limited AI GPU supply.

cards.title: A single leading-edge chip fab costs upwards of $20 billion to build.
cards.detail: Cleanrooms, EUV scanners and hundreds of other tools drive the price. That cost is why only three companies — TSMC, Samsung and Intel — compete at the frontier.

cards.statement: Since 2022, the US has restricted exports of top AI GPUs and chipmaking tools to China.
cards.why: True. Rules issued in October 2022 and tightened since limit sales of advanced accelerators and the equipment to make leading-edge chips, aiming to slow China's frontier AI and military computing.
